sm: Host Tim Rice welcomes three Daily Wire reporters who have been nominated for the Dow Prize, an annual award for investigative journalism now in its fourth year. The Daily Wire has the most nominations of any outlet this year, four in all, because Luke Rosiak was nominated twice. Jenny Tarr's multimedia nomination is a mini documentary made in Minneapolis, where she embedded with ICE agents during large anti-ICE disruptions. Megan Brock obtained a 78 page plan to transform social welfare agencies with gender ideology, which she says the Biden administration had already begun carrying out. Luke Rosiak's Medicaid series covers home health fraud in Columbus, Ohio, which led to testimony before Congress and a change in state law.

Rice says the three stories revive classic investigative journalism by exposing things the public needs to know, whatever the political implications. Rosiak says the work is interesting by definition and carries a thrill of the chase, though it can feel negative. He hopes that exposing fraud pushes policymakers to act. Brock says she loves public records, likening them to a puzzle, and says she wants to tell her grandchildren she did what she could. Tarr describes the hostile scene in Minneapolis, with whistles, shouting and agitators who followed ICE and foiled an arrest attempt. She says the stories from ICE officers' own perspective, including their early mornings and six day weeks, are often untold.

Rice asks how the reporters see their work in a changing media landscape that includes citizen journalists. Rosiak says outlets like the New York Times do rigorous work apart from their liberal bias, so old school reporting is worth keeping. Brock says citizen journalists sometimes do good work, including undercover video, but they often fail to ask for comment and cannot spend months on one story. She says the Daily Wire combines speed with depth, and that the Dow Prize is something like the Pulitzer Prize of non-liberal media, with a top prize of about 100,000 dollars. Tarr tells of walking into the Houston house linked to the New Orleans attack after the FBI left it open, while other media stood far off. She adds that citizen journalists often become the story and do not assess risk.

Rice asks how the midterm results, with Democrats strengthened in Congress and a presidential race ahead, will change their targets. Rosiak says he will cover Democratic scandals because those stories are less picked over, but he will focus on policy and fraud, since Republicans still run the executive branch and can act on his findings. He recounts his earlier reporting on the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service, ignored under Obama but later shut down after the fraud task force and Doge found it. Brock says medical institutions still push gender ideology, ballot measures in Washington and Colorado succeeded, and Democrats will struggle to distance themselves from it. Tarr expects sanctuary city ordinances and political shifts in Texas. Rice thanks them and closes the episode.
